question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below
Amalgamate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Dismantle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Amalgamate" means to combine or merge two or more things (organizations, elements, ideas) into one unified whole. (मिलाना/एकीकृत करना)
◦ Example: The two small banks decided to amalgamate into a single larger institution.

• Its antonym is "Dismantle", which means to take something apart / to break up a structure or organisation piece by piece. (अलग करना/तोड़ना)
◦ Example: The workers began to dismantle the old factory machinery.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Integrate" is incorrect because it is a synonym, not an antonym, of "Amalgamate" — it means to combine parts into a whole.

• Option 3: "Coalesce" is incorrect because it is also a synonym of "Amalgamate" — it means to come together and form one mass or whole.

• Option 4: "Combine" is incorrect because it too means to join together, making it a synonym rather than an opposite of "Amalgamate".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Amalgamate": merge, unite, blend, fuse, consolidate.

• Other antonyms of "Amalgamate": separate, divide, disperse, segregate, disunite.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
He said, “I will go to Indonesia tomorrow”.
option_1: He said he would go to Indonesia by tomorrow.
option_2: He said that he would go to Indonesia tomorrow.
option_3: He said that he would be going to Indonesia the next day.
option_4: He said that he would go to Indonesia the next day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He said that he would go to Indonesia the next day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is in Direct Speech, Simple Future Tense, with the reporting verb "said" in the past tense.

• Rule — Change of tense and time expressions in Indirect Speech:
◦ When the reporting verb is in the past tense, "will" changes to "would".
◦ Time expressions also shift: "tomorrow" changes to "the next day" (or "the following day").

• Applying the rule: "I will go to Indonesia tomorrow" becomes "he would go to Indonesia the next day", and since the reporting verb is followed by a full clause, the connector "that" is used.
◦ Indirect: He said that he would go to Indonesia the next day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it inserts "by" before "tomorrow" — apart from not converting "tomorrow", "by tomorrow" also changes the original meaning (deadline sense) which is not present in the direct speech.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it retains "tomorrow" instead of changing it to "the next day", which is grammatically wrong once the reporting verb "said" is in the past.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it uses "would be going" (future continuous form), whereas the direct speech uses the simple future "will go", which must become the simple "would go", not a continuous form.

NOTE

• Common time-expression changes in indirect speech: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, this → that, these → those, here → there, ago → before.

• Modal changes: will → would, can → could, may → might, must → had to/must.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
She told me to wait here.
option_1: I am told to wait here by her.
option_2: I was told to wait there by her.
option_3: I was told to waited here by her.
option_4: I was told to wait here by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I was told to wait here by her.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "She told me to wait here" is in the Simple Past Tense and follows the pattern Subject + told + Object + Infinitive (to + V1).

• Rule — Passive of "Subject + told/asked/ordered + Object + to + V1":
◦ Active: Subject + told + Object + to + V1
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + told + to + V1 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "me" becomes the subject "I"; since it is singular and the tense is past, the auxiliary used is "was"; the infinitive "to wait" and the adverb "here" are retained unchanged; and "she" becomes the agent "by her".
◦ Passive: I was told to wait here by her.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it uses "am told" (present tense), whereas the original sentence is in the past tense and must remain "was told".

• Option 2 is incorrect because it changes "here" to "there", which alters the meaning of the original sentence; place adverbs like "here" are retained as they are (unless the reporting itself requires a shift, which is not the case in a simple passive transformation).

• Option 3 is incorrect because it wrongly uses "to waited" instead of the correct infinitive form "to wait" — the infinitive "to + V1" never takes a past-tense verb.

NOTE

• Verbs like tell, ask, order, request, allow, permit, advise followed by an object and an infinitive follow the same passive pattern: Object + was/were + V3 + to + V1 + by + Subject.

• Adverbs of place/time (here, there, now, today) are not changed in a simple active-to-passive transformation — they only change in reported/indirect speech.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A religions war
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Crusade.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Crusade" means a war or military campaign undertaken in the name of religion, especially the medieval Christian expeditions to recover the Holy Land; more broadly, it also means a vigorous campaign for a cause. (धर्म युद्ध)
◦ Example: The medieval Crusade was fought between Christians and Muslims over control of Jerusalem.

• The phrase given, "a religious war", is exactly the literal meaning of "Crusade", making it the correct one-word substitution.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Colloquial" (बोलचाल की भाषा से संबंधित): relating to informal, everyday spoken language — unrelated to war.

• Option 3: "Inscription" (उत्कीर्ण लेख): words carved, engraved, or imprinted on a surface such as stone or metal — unrelated to war.

• Option 4: "Colonialism" (उपनिवेशवाद): the policy or practice of a country acquiring control over another territory or people — related to political domination, not specifically a religious war.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often asked in SSC: Anarchy (absence of government/law), Mutiny (organised rebellion against authority, especially military), Coup (sudden overthrow of a government), Insurgency (an organised rebellion against an established authority)

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
A disconsolate Arjun ______ his way back down the mountain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. makes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "makes his way" is a fixed idiomatic collocation meaning to proceed or travel, typically with some effort or in a particular direction/manner.
◦ Example: The exhausted climber made his way back to the base camp.

• Rule — Collocation with "way": the verb "make" habitually collocates with the noun "way" to describe movement (make one's way, find one's way, lose one's way, wind one's way). No other common verb pairs naturally with "way" in this sense.

• Applying this to the sentence: "A disconsolate Arjun makes his way back down the mountain" correctly uses this standard collocation to describe Arjun's dejected walk back down.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "deserts" is incorrect because "desert" (to abandon) is a transitive verb that takes a direct object like a place or person (e.g., "deserts the mountain"); it cannot take "his way" as its object in this collocation sense.

• Option 3: "elopes" is incorrect because "elope" means to run away secretly to get married, which is meaningless in the context of walking down a mountain, and "elope" is intransitive — it cannot be followed by "his way".

• Option 4: "absconds" is incorrect because "abscond" means to flee secretly, typically to avoid arrest or an obligation; it is intransitive and does not collocate with "his way", and it does not fit the neutral act of walking back down a mountain.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with "way": make one's way, find one's way, lose one's way, feel one's way, wind one's way, work one's way, pave the way.

• "Desert" and "abscond" both relate to leaving/fleeing but differ in register: desert = to abandon (a person, post, or duty); abscond = to flee secretly, usually to evade the law or a duty.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. the shape of an egg has been highly regarded for its evolution
Q. the body in the most efficient way, not roll away once laid, is structurally
R. as large enough to incubate an embryo, small enough to exit
S. sound enough to bear weight and be the beginning of life for so many species
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. PRQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In a sentence-rearrangement (para jumble) question, the correct order is found by identifying the part that introduces the main subject, then tracing the logical/grammatical chain that follows from it.

• Part P — "the shape of an egg has been highly regarded for its evolution" — introduces the subject (the shape of an egg) and must come first, since every other part explains why the shape is so regarded.

• Part R — "as large enough to incubate an embryo, small enough to exit" — logically follows P, continuing the reason ("regarded for its evolution as...") and beginning the list of qualities.

• Part Q — "the body in the most efficient way, not roll away once laid, is structurally" — grammatically completes R's incomplete clause ("small enough to exit the body...") and leads into the final descriptive clause with "is structurally".

• Part S — "sound enough to bear weight and be the beginning of life for so many species" — completes the sentence, following naturally after "is structurally" in Q ("is structurally sound enough...").

• Combined: "The shape of an egg has been highly regarded for its evolution as large enough to incubate an embryo, small enough to exit the body in the most efficient way, not roll away once laid, is structurally sound enough to bear weight and be the beginning of life for so many species."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (PRQS).

Additional Information

• Option 1: SPQR is incorrect because it begins with S ("sound enough to bear weight..."), which is a concluding clause and cannot logically open the sentence without an antecedent subject.

• Option 2: QPRS is incorrect because it places Q, which depends grammatically on R ("small enough to exit the body..."), before both P and R, breaking the required cause-and-effect sequence.

• Option 4: PSQR is incorrect because although it correctly starts with P, placing S immediately after P disconnects "regarded for its evolution" from the list of qualities (R) that explain it, producing a disjointed sentence.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, look for grammatical continuity clues — an incomplete phrase in one part (like "exit ___" in R) is usually completed by a specific other part (like "the body" in Q).

• Also look for pronoun/article references and logical cause-effect or chronological order to fix the correct sequence.

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: The cursor must be plased at the strat of the line.
option_2: The cursor must be placed at the start of the line.
option_3: The cursur must be placed at the start of the line.
option_4: The cursor must be plased at the start of the line.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The cursor must be placed at the start of the line.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This sentence contains no spelling errors: "cursor" (not "cursur"), "placed" (not "plased"), and "start" (not "strat") are all spelled correctly.

• Rule: In "choose the sentence with no spelling error" questions, examine each key word across all four options individually, since the same word is often misspelled in different ways in different options — cross-checking word by word (not sentence by sentence) is the fastest method.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The cursor must be plased at the strat of the line." is incorrect because "plased" should be "placed" and "strat" should be "start".

• Option 3: "The cursur must be placed at the start of the line." is incorrect because "cursur" should be "cursor".

• Option 4: "The cursor must be plased at the start of the line." is incorrect because "plased" should be "placed".

NOTE

• Commonly confused spellings in SSC exams: cursor (not cursur), placed (not plased), necessary (not neccessary), occurred (not occured), separate (not seperate), definitely (not definately).

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Remedy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Panacea.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Remedy" means a medicine or treatment for a disease or problem; a solution to a difficulty. (उपचार/समाधान)
◦ Example: Rest and warm fluids are a simple remedy for the common cold.

• The closest match is "Panacea", which means a solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases; a cure-all. (सर्वरोगहर/रामबाण इलाज)
◦ Example: Technology is often wrongly seen as a panacea for every social problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Plagiarism" (साहित्यिक चोरी): the act of copying someone else's work or ideas and passing them off as one's own — unrelated in meaning to "remedy".

• Option 2: "Tablet" (गोली/पट्टिका): either a pill/medicine dose or a flat slab for writing/inscription — a specific object, not a synonym for the general concept of a "remedy" or "solution".

• Option 3: "Parochial" (संकुचित/स्थानीय): having a narrow or limited outlook, concerned only with a small area — unrelated to "remedy".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Remedy": cure, solution, antidote, treatment, panacea, corrective.

• Do not confuse "Panacea" (a cure for everything) with "Placebo" (a substance with no therapeutic effect, given to satisfy a patient) — both relate to medicine but mean very different things.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Nark
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Irritate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Nark" (informal, chiefly British usage) as a verb means to annoy or irritate someone. (चिढ़ाना/जलन पैदा करना)
◦ Example: It really narks me when people talk loudly during a film.

• The closest synonym among the options is "Irritate", meaning to annoy or make someone impatient or angry. (चिढ़ाना)
◦ Example: His constant complaining began to irritate his colleagues.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Obligation" (कर्तव्य/बाध्यता): a duty or commitment to do something — unrelated in meaning to "nark".

• Option 3: "Reassure" (आश्वस्त करना): to say or do something to remove someone's doubts or fears — this is nearly opposite in tone to the irritation implied by "nark".

• Option 4: "Solace" (सांत्वना): comfort or consolation in a time of distress — again, roughly opposite to the irritation meant by "nark".

NOTE

• As a noun, "nark" (British slang) also means an informer, especially a police informer — a different but related informal sense of the word.

• Other synonyms for "irritate": annoy, vex, exasperate, needle, provoke, rile.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Have people rolling in the aisles
option_2: To use false promises to pull people on one's side
option_3: To have a dispute with someone
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Make an audience laugh uncontrollably.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Have people rolling in the aisles" means to make an audience laugh so hard that they can barely control themselves, as if they were rolling about with laughter in the aisles of a theatre. (दर्शकों को खूब हंसाना)
◦ Example: The stand-up comedian had the whole audience rolling in the aisles with his jokes.

• The expression comes from theatre/cinema settings, where "aisles" are the walkways between rows of seats — the image is of people laughing so hard they nearly fall out of their seats into the aisle.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Willing to do something immediately" describes eagerness or readiness, which is unrelated to laughter or audiences.

• Option 2: "To use false promises to pull people on one's side" describes deceitful persuasion, which has no connection to the idiom's meaning of causing laughter.

• Option 3: "To have a dispute with someone" describes a quarrel or conflict, which is unrelated to the idea of amusing an audience.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to laughter/humour often asked in SSC: "Split one's sides (laughing)" (to laugh very hard), "Laugh one's head off" (to laugh uncontrollably), "Crack a joke" (to tell a joke), "Die laughing" (to laugh extremely hard).

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The shelf is too highest for me to reach.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. too high.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence uses "too highest", which incorrectly combines the intensifier "too" with a superlative degree adjective — this is grammatically wrong.

• Rule — "Too" + Adjective/Adverb (Positive Degree): the word "too" (meaning "excessively") is always followed by the positive (base) degree of an adjective or adverb, never the comparative or superlative degree. Pattern: too + adjective (positive degree) + to + V1.

• Applying the rule: since "shelf" needs the adjective form (describing height, a physical quality of the shelf, not a verb), "high" (positive degree adjective) is correct: "The shelf is too high for me to reach."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because "too highest" is ungrammatical — "too" cannot combine with a superlative form.

• Option 3: "more higher" is incorrect because it creates a double comparative ("more" + "higher"), which is grammatically wrong; only one comparative marker should be used at a time.

• Option 4: "too highly" is incorrect because "highly" is an adverb (meaning "very" or "extremely", used with abstract ideas like "highly regarded"), whereas the sentence needs an adjective to describe the physical height of the shelf, not an adverb.

NOTE

• "Too" always takes the positive degree: too big, too fast, too expensive — never "too biggest" or "too faster".

• Distinguish "high" (adjective, e.g., a high shelf / adverb of physical height, e.g., "flew high") from "highly" (adverb of degree, used for abstract qualities, e.g., "highly qualified", "highly regarded").

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.
The Event Horizon Telescope can help scientists analyse the shapes and behaviours
of event horizons.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The Event Horizon Telescope can help scientists analyse the shapes and behaviours of event horizons" is grammatically correct as it stands.

• Rule — "Help" + Object + Bare Infinitive: the verb "help" can be correctly followed by an object and either a bare infinitive (V1 without "to") or a to-infinitive — both "help scientists analyse" and "help scientists to analyse" are grammatically acceptable in modern English.

• The modal "can" is correctly followed by the base form "help", the noun phrase "shapes and behaviours" are correctly joined by "and", and the preposition "of" correctly links to "event horizons".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "help scientists analyse the shapes" is not an error, since "help + object + bare infinitive" is a standard, accepted grammatical structure.

• Option 2: "The Event Horizon Telescope can" is not an error, since the modal "can" is correctly followed by a base-form verb ("help") later in the sentence.

• Option 3: "and behaviours of event horizons." is not an error, since "behaviours" is correctly used as the plural noun paired with "shapes", and the preposition "of" correctly introduces what the shapes and behaviours belong to.

NOTE

• Verbs that can be followed by a bare infinitive after an object include: help, make, let, see, hear, feel, watch (e.g., "let him go", "make her cry", "help us finish").

• In error-spotting questions, always check the sentence is complete and consistent even when no single part looks obviously wrong — "No error" is frequently the correct choice when the sentence follows a valid, accepted grammatical pattern.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose ‘No improvement’ as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
They weren't allows to take their dog into the store.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. allowed to take.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence uses "weren't allows to take", which is grammatically incorrect — after the auxiliary "weren't" (were + not), a past participle (V3) is required to form the passive voice, not a base-form verb.

• Rule — Passive Voice with "was/were": the structure is Subject + was/were (+ not) + V3 (past participle) + .... Since the subject "They" is plural and the sentence is in the past tense, "weren't" must be followed by the past participle "allowed".

• Applying the rule: "They weren't allowed to take their dog into the store" — "allowed" (V3) is followed correctly by the infinitive "to take" (V1), since "allow" itself takes a to-infinitive as its complement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "allow to take" is incorrect because "allow" (base form) does not agree with the auxiliary "weren't", which requires the past participle "allowed".

• Option 2: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original phrase "allows to take" is ungrammatical after "weren't".

• Option 3: "allowed to took" is incorrect because although "allowed" is correctly used, "took" (a simple past form) cannot follow "to" — the infinitive must be "to take" (V1), not a past-tense verb.

NOTE

• After was/were (+not), always use the past participle (V3) to form the passive: was/were + told/asked/allowed/permitted/seen/taken, etc.

• The verb "allow" is followed by object + to-infinitive: allow someone to do something (not "to did/took" etc.).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
In the flesh
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. In bodily form.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "In the flesh" means in person; physically present, as opposed to seen on screen, in a photo, or imagined. (साक्षात्/स्वयं प्रत्यक्ष रूप में)
◦ Example: I've seen him on television many times, but this was the first time I met him in the flesh.

• The phrase emphasises actual, physical bodily presence — "flesh" here refers to the physical body itself, distinguishing a real, live appearance from a virtual or indirect one.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To be near death" (मृत्यु के निकट होना): this describes a critical medical condition, unrelated to physical presence.

• Option 3: "To get a tattoo" (टैटू बनवाना): this refers to having permanent ink markings put on the skin — unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 4: "To talk" (बात करना): this simply means to speak or converse, unrelated to the idea of physical presence conveyed by "in the flesh".

NOTE

• Other idioms using body-related words often asked in SSC: "In cold blood" (without mercy/deliberately), "To one's heart's content" (as much as one desires), "By the skin of one's teeth" (very narrowly), "To have a bone to pick" (to have a grievance to discuss).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
I believe that we are ________ responsible for our choices.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. solely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adverb "solely" means only, exclusively, entirely — it is commonly used with the adjective "responsible" to emphasise that responsibility belongs to one party alone, with no sharing of blame.
◦ Example: She is solely responsible for organising the entire event.

• Rule — Collocation: "responsible" frequently pairs with intensifying/limiting adverbs such as solely, entirely, wholly, partly, jointly to specify the degree or exclusivity of responsibility. Among the given options, only "solely" fits this collocational and logical pattern.

• Applying this to the sentence: "I believe that we are solely responsible for our choices" correctly conveys that responsibility rests entirely with "we" (the subject), with no external excuse.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "durably" means "in a way that lasts a long time" (e.g., durably built) — it does not logically modify "responsible", since responsibility is not measured in terms of durability.

• Option 2: "ordinarily" means "usually, under normal circumstances" — while grammatically possible, it does not carry the emphatic, natural collocation with "responsible" that "solely" does, and changes the intended meaning of the sentence (from "exclusively" to "in general").

• Option 4: "profusely" means "in large amounts, abundantly" (typically used with words like "apologise", "sweat", "thank") — it does not collocate meaningfully with "responsible".

NOTE

• Common adverb + "responsible" collocations in SSC vocabulary questions: solely responsible, wholly responsible, jointly responsible, directly responsible, personally responsible.

• "Profusely" is most often tested with verbs like apologise profusely, bleed profusely, sweat profusely, thank profusely.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A slight fault that can be forgiven
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Venial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Venial" means a minor fault, error or sin that is easily excused or forgiven, as opposed to a serious or unforgivable one. (क्षम्य/मामूली)
◦ Example: Forgetting to reply to an email is a venial mistake, not a serious offence.

• The given phrase, "a slight fault that can be forgiven", matches exactly with the meaning of "Venial", making it the correct one-word substitution.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Libel" (मानहानि/लांछन): a published false statement that damages a person's reputation — a legal/defamation term, unrelated to a "forgivable fault".

• Option 3: "Libertine" (स्वच्छंदी व्यक्ति): a person who behaves without moral restraint, especially in sexual matters — describes a type of person, not a minor fault.

• Option 4: "Referral" (संदर्भ/सिफारिश): the act of directing someone to another person or place for information, help, or treatment — completely unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• The direct opposite of "Venial" is "Mortal" (as in "mortal sin" — a grave, unforgivable wrong), or more generally "unpardonable/inexcusable".

• Related one-word substitutions: Culpable (deserving blame), Condone (to forgive or overlook an offence), Absolve (to free from blame or guilt).

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Trnuk.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Trnuk" is an incorrectly spelt word — the correct spelling is "Trunk", referring to the main stem of a tree, the long nose of an elephant, or a large storage box, among other meanings.

• Rule: In "choose the incorrectly spelt word" questions, check each option individually against its standard dictionary spelling — a single misplaced or missing letter (as in "Trnuk" for "Trunk", where the "u" and "n" are transposed) is a common error type tested by SSC.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Dinner" is correctly spelt — the main evening meal.

• Option 3: "Blade" is correctly spelt — the flat cutting part of a knife or similar tool.

• Option 4: "Mentor" is correctly spelt — a trusted advisor or guide.

NOTE

• Watch for letter transposition errors (like "Trnuk" for "Trunk") — SSC frequently tests these by swapping two adjacent letters in an otherwise familiar word.

• Practice commonly transposed-letter words: "recieve" (receive), "freind" (friend), "wierd" (weird), "adress" (address).

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.
If you doesn't have a doctor, contact your public health authority.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. If you doesn't have.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in "If you doesn't have" — this is a subject-verb agreement error.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "You": the pronoun "you" (whether singular or plural in meaning) always takes the base-form auxiliary "do/don't" in the present tense, never "does/doesn't", which is reserved for third-person singular subjects (he, she, it, or a singular noun).

• Applying the rule: the correct form is "If you don't have a doctor, contact your public health authority."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "your public health authority." is not an error — the phrase is grammatically correct as the object of "contact".

• Option 2: "a doctor, contact" is not an error — the comma correctly separates the conditional clause from the imperative main clause ("contact...").

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect because there IS an identifiable error, i.e., "doesn't" instead of "don't", in part 4 of the sentence.

NOTE

• "You" always pairs with do/don't, have/haven't, are/aren't — never with the third-person singular forms "does/doesn't", "has/hasn't", "is/isn't".

• Third-person singular subjects (he, she, it, and singular nouns) require does, has, is in the present tense — e.g., "He doesn't have", "She has", "It is".

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. Select the option 'no correction required' if the sentence is correct as given.
The palace was in turmoil because Sikhandi (had return.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. had returned.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed segment "had return" is grammatically incorrect — after the auxiliary "had", a past participle (V3) form of the verb is required, not the base form.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense: the structure is Subject + had + V3 (past participle) + ..., used to describe an action completed before another past action or state. Here, "the palace was in turmoil" (past) resulted from an earlier completed action, i.e., Sikhandi's return, which must therefore be expressed in the past perfect.

• Applying the rule: the past participle of "return" is "returned", so the correct form is "had returned": "The palace was in turmoil because Sikhandi had returned."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "have turned" is incorrect because "have" does not agree with the past-tense context of the sentence (which requires "had"), and "turned" is also the wrong verb — the sentence is about Sikhandi's "return", not "turn".

• Option 2: "No correction required" is incorrect because the original phrase "had return" is ungrammatical, since "had" must be followed by a past participle ("returned"), not the base form ("return").

• Option 4: "was return" is incorrect because "was" (a form of "be") cannot be directly followed by a base-form verb like "return" to form a sensible tense in this context.

NOTE

• Past Perfect Tense (had + V3) is used for an action that happened before another past action — often signalled by words like "because", "after", "before", "already", "by the time".

• Common irregular past participles tested in SSC: go → gone, do → done, see → seen, break → broken, write → written, take → taken.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Nascence
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Incipience.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Nascence" means the process of being born or coming into existence; the beginning or origin of something. (जन्म/उत्पत्ति/आरंभ)
◦ Example: The nascence of the internet can be traced back to research projects in the 1960s.

• The closest synonym is "Incipience", which means the initial or beginning stage of something's existence. (आरंभिक अवस्था/शुरुआत)
◦ Example: The idea was still in its incipience when they first discussed it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Cessation" (समाप्ति/रुकावट): the fact or process of ending or being brought to an end — this is nearly opposite in meaning to "Nascence" (beginning vs. ending).

• Option 2: "Acrimonious" (कटु/तीखा): an adjective describing bitter and angry speech or disputes — unrelated to the idea of beginning or birth.

• Option 4: "Omega" (अंत/अंतिम): the last letter of the Greek alphabet, used figuratively to mean "the end" or "the last of something" — this is the opposite of "Nascence", which means a beginning.

NOTE

• Related word: "Nascent" (adjective) means just beginning to exist or develop, e.g., "a nascent democracy".

• Common antonym pairs tested with beginnings/endings: Genesis ↔ Demise, Inception ↔ Termination, Nascence ↔ Cessation/Omega.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she's steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. refused.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "put my foot down" means to take a firm stand or insist on something, usually going against what others expect or want.

• In this context, the narrator normally would be expected to apply to the "Best School" (Harvard), following in the footsteps of the family's usual ambition (as hinted later — Charlie already went there and was suspended). Instead, "for once", the narrator takes a firm stand and refuses to apply there, choosing Yale, the "Second-Best School," instead.

• "Refused to apply" logically connects with "put my foot down" — both describe an act of firm resistance against an expectation, and fits the following sentence describing this decision as "a bridge entirely too far" from the family/brother's path.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "dwelled" means "lived in a place" or "thought/talked about something at length" — neither sense logically completes "put my foot down and dwelled to apply", which is grammatically and contextually odd (the verb "dwell" is not typically followed by a "to-infinitive" in this sense).

• Option 3: "levelled" means "made flat" or "aimed (a criticism/accusation)" — it does not fit meaningfully with "put my foot down and levelled to apply".

• Option 4: "rejoiced" means "felt or expressed great joy" — this contradicts the tone of firm, somewhat reluctant resistance implied by "put my foot down", and does not fit grammatically with "to apply" in this context.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, the blank must fit both grammatically and contextually — always read the full surrounding sentence(s), not just the immediate phrase, since later details (like Charlie's suspension) often confirm the intended sense.

• "Put one's foot down" is a common idiom in SSC comprehension/cloze passages meaning to be firm or decisive, often used before describing an assertive or contrary decision.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she's steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. being.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Gerund after a Preposition: when a verb follows a preposition (here, "of"), it must take the -ing (gerund) form, not the base form, an infinitive, or a perfect participle construction with "having been".

• Applying the rule: "The idea of being Charlie's younger brother..." correctly uses the gerund "being" after the preposition "of", meaning "the idea of [someone] being Charlie's younger brother [enrolled] at another school".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "be" is incorrect because the base form of the verb cannot directly follow a preposition like "of" — only the gerund (-ing) form can.

• Option 2: "having been" is incorrect because this perfect gerund form implies a completed action before another past action, which does not fit the simple, ongoing sense of "being someone's brother [at a school]" intended here; it is also unnecessarily complex for the context.

• Option 4: "been" is incorrect because "been" is a past participle and cannot stand alone directly after a preposition without an auxiliary like "having".

NOTE

• Prepositions are always followed by gerunds (-ing forms), never by base verbs or infinitives — e.g., "interested in learning", "good at swimming", "afraid of falling".

• Common cloze-test trap: distinguishing simple gerund ("being") from perfect gerund ("having been") — use the perfect gerund only when emphasising that one action was completed before another past action.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she's steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. who.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Who knows" is a common fixed expression meaning "nobody can say for certain" or used rhetorically to express uncertainty; here, "who" functions as the subject of the verb "knows".

• Rule — Relative/Interrogative Pronoun Case: "who" is used as a subject pronoun (performing the action of the verb), while "whom" is used as an object pronoun (receiving the action). Since "who/whom" here is the doer of the action "knows", the subject form "who" is required.

• Applying the rule: "who knows if Harvard would even take me" — "who" is the subject of "knows", making it grammatically correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "whom" is incorrect because "whom" is an object pronoun and cannot serve as the subject of the verb "knows".

• Option 2: "which" is incorrect because "which" is used to refer to things or animals, not to people (or to a general/impersonal "anybody" sense) as intended by "who knows" here.

• Option 4: "whose" is incorrect because "whose" is a possessive pronoun/determiner (indicating ownership) and does not fit the sentence, which requires a subject pronoun before the verb "knows".

NOTE

• Quick memory trick: "who" = he/she/they (subject); "whom" = him/her/them (object). If you can replace the pronoun with "he", use "who"; if with "him", use "whom".

• The idiomatic phrase "who knows" is commonly used to mean "it is uncertain" and always takes the subject form "who", never "whom".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she's steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. I.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Subject Pronoun in a Compound Subject: when a pronoun is joined with a noun (like "My mom and ___") to form the subject of a sentence, the subject-case pronoun must be used, i.e., "I", not the object-case "me" or the reflexive "myself".

• Applying the rule: "My mom and I are in the kitchen" — here, "My mom and I" together form the subject of the verb "are", so the subject pronoun "I" is correct.

• A simple test: remove "My mom and" from the sentence — "I am in the kitchen" (correct) versus "Me am in the kitchen" (incorrect) confirms that "I" is the right choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "me" is incorrect because "me" is an object-case pronoun, used only when the pronoun receives the action of a verb or follows a preposition, not when it is part of the subject.

• Option 2: "am" is incorrect because it is a verb, not a pronoun, and cannot logically follow "and" to complete the noun phrase "My mom and ___"; it also creates a subject-verb agreement clash with the plural verb "are" later in the sentence.

• Option 3: "myself" is incorrect because "myself" is a reflexive/emphatic pronoun, used only when it refers back to a subject already mentioned in the same clause (e.g., "I did it myself"), not as a standalone subject alongside a noun.

NOTE

• Common error to avoid: many speakers mistakenly use "me" in compound subjects (e.g., "Me and my mom are...") — always test by removing the other noun/pronoun to check which case is grammatically correct.

• Similarly, in compound objects, the object case is required: "Give it to my mom and me" (not "I").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Today I have a college admission interview with a Yale alum. Yale is Second-Best School, but for once, I put my foot down and (1) ______ to apply to Best School (Harvard). The idea of (2) ______ Charlie's younger brother at another school is a bridge entirely too far. Besides, (3) ______ knows if Harvard would even take me now that Charlie's been suspended. My mom and (4) ______ are in the kitchen. Because of my interview, she's steaming frozen mandu (dumplings) for me as a treat. I am having a pre-mandu appetizer of Cap'n Crunch (the best cereal known to mankind) and (5) ______ in my Moleskine notebook.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. writing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Parallel Structure with Present Continuous Tense: the sentence begins with "I am having..." (present continuous), and the second action joined by "and" must also be in a form parallel to this continuous construction, i.e., an -ing form, to describe an action happening at the same time.

• Applying the rule: "I am having a pre-mandu appetizer... and writing in my Moleskine notebook" — "writing" (an -ing form, parallel to "having") logically and grammatically completes the sentence, describing the narrator's simultaneous action of jotting something down in a notebook while eating a snack before the interview.

• Contextually, using a notebook to jot notes/thoughts before an interview also makes "writing" the most sensible action among the choices.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "visualising" is grammatically parallel (-ing form) but contextually odd — one does not typically "visualise... in a notebook"; visualising is a mental process, not something done physically inside a notebook.

• Option 2: "sieving" means straining a substance through a sieve (e.g., flour) — this does not fit the context of "in my Moleskine notebook" at all.

• Option 4: "reading" is grammatically possible (-ing form) but less contextually fitting than "writing", since a Moleskine notebook is primarily associated with writing notes/journaling (and the earlier context about "interview" preparation), and this is the standard best-fit answer per the passage/answer key.

NOTE

• In cloze passages testing parallel structure, always check that all verbs joined by "and"/"or" share the same grammatical form (all -ing, all base form, or all to-infinitives).

• A Moleskine notebook is a well-known brand of notebook commonly associated with journaling, sketching, and note-writing — a useful contextual clue in comprehension passages.
